“Dizzy with happiness, girl?” Susie said. “Say yes. Get engaged first, then after graduation you can have a grand wedding. I reserve the bridesmaid's job!”
“Oh, come on, I have to play hard to get a little! And look how sudden it is. I haven't even brushed my teeth... How can I accept a proposal like this?”
“Look at you, tail in the air!” Susie laughed and pushed her head under the water.
Caught off guard, Nono choked on a mouthful of water. Everything suddenly went black.
“Oh no!” She was still conscious.

Since the Three Gorges operation she had kept having dreams. The doctor said it was a minor aftereffect of prolonged oxygen deprivation underwater and would gradually heal. But Nono hated this “minor” aftereffect, because it was always the same dream.

In the dream all was a blue so dark it was nearly black. Light came down through the water overhead, its ripples reflected across her face. She floated amid endless waves, unable even to hear her own heartbeat. Figures seemed to move above the surface. She tried to rise but had no strength, unable to move a finger. They seemed to bend over her with grief-stricken faces. She felt as though she lay in a coffin, saying goodbye to loved ones through glass.

What a nightmare, how she hated it! Time didn't flow in the dream. It was so cold; she wanted fearfully to curl up but lacked the strength. It was so quiet; she wanted to talk to someone but couldn't speak. It was so hopeless. So this was what death was like.
Every time she woke she was cold all over. She didn't remember what had happened underwater at the Three Gorges, but she understood the dream was about death.
The moment she choked on the water she saw that almost-black blue again. She floated in endless waves, unable to move. The damned lack of oxygen had dragged her bodily into the dream!
She felt she was going to die...

Everything suddenly tore apart! Water, light, the almost-black blue, everything was ripped open by claws! As if the vault of heaven had split, an enormous face appeared in the gap, with golden eyes bright as day! That twisted, ferocious... child's face...
“Don't die!” he roared.
“Ricar...do.” Nono called out the name.
More water flooded her throat. She kicked hard several times, found her footing in the spring, and gasped, her eyes filled with terror.
“Oh, sorry, sorry!” Susie hurried to help her.

Susie hadn't expected such an accomplished swimmer to come to grief in this little pool. Nono had clearly swallowed several mouthfuls, not just the first one; she'd swallowed more while struggling and calling out underwater. Susie hadn't heard what she said, but through the surface had seen the terror on her face. In all the time they'd known each other, she had never seen the little red-haired witch so shaken.
“I'm fine, I'm fine.” Nono waved a hand and turned, forcing a smile for Susie. “I'm a little dizzy. I'll sit in the sauna.”
Susie watched her white-swimsuited back disappear into the darkness, suddenly feeling as though she had become another person.
Nono was alone in the sauna. She ladled cool water over the red-hot stones; dense steam spread and blurred her vision.

The phone screen was the only thing she could see clearly through the steam. It displayed a multimedia message she had already prepared. She had hesitated to send it, thought it inappropriate, then couldn't quite bear to cancel it. So the message remained in her drafts, its fate dependent on her mood.
The message was a song: “Happy birthday to you, Ri-Ricardo, happy birthday to you, Ri-Ricardo...”
On the way to Hailuogou, the tune had suddenly occurred to her. She had recorded it for fun, thinking she'd send it to Lu Mingfei on his birthday and he'd surely grin like an idiot.

But... did it suggest something, however faintly? She rarely hesitated; she generally did whatever came to mind. And was there any need to hesitate? She couldn't possibly like Lu Mingfei. At most she pitied him a little. When they first met he was a genuine beaten dog, and the image of him crouching alone in a corner, gasping for breath, felt familiar. She had already been quite good to him; having a pretty senior looking out for him would make college easier. She hated seeing anyone helpless. As for his liking her, surely it would pass? Wasn't a junior supposed to learn how girls thought from his senior, then use that knowledge to charm girls younger than himself?
Just as the older men who praised her in kindergarten belonged with women their own age, a junior belonged with a younger girl.

She should have been happily bouncing around today, getting thoroughly drunk with Susie tonight. It was the first proposal of her life... So why had that childish face suddenly appeared? She'd never seen him so frantic, furious, and ferocious. That wasn't an expression he should wear. Suddenly all her joy had faded, leaving her very, very tired.
She sat silently in the steam. Today was Lu Mingfei's birthday; in half an hour it would be over.
Lu Mingfei took out his phone and checked the time: 11:30 p.m. Rain streamed past the airplane window, and the city's scattered lights could be seen in the distance.

Chu Zihang handed him a small packet. “This route crosses the Arctic Circle. Ten hours; sleep and you'll be in Chicago.” Then he briskly put in earplugs, covered his eyes with a mask, fitted an inflatable neck pillow, pulled up a blanket, and fell asleep.
Lu Mingfei opened the packet. Inside was an identical set. Chu Zihang had long since planned to spend the ten-hour flight resting; the man's life was precise as a machine.
“United Airlines Flight UA836 to Chicago is preparing for departure. Please switch off your mobile communication devices.” A sweet female voice echoed through the cabin.

No new messages came. Lu Mingfei pressed the power button until the screen went black. What was the person he was thinking of doing at this moment? Better not wonder about what he couldn't know. Perhaps she was nestled beside someone, fishing on the sunlit Red Sea, while he thought of her on a dark rainy night. It made him seem so humble, wrapped in a gloomy, unpleasant haze, didn't it? Lu Mingfei put in his earplugs and eye mask. Darkness filled his vision, and the enormous roar of the engines was shut out; all he could feel was the acceleration and vibration of his seat. The Boeing 747 pierced the curtain of rain and climbed diagonally into the sky, skimming over the sleeping city.
“Good night,” Lu Mingfei said softly, not knowing to whom.
